Assistant District Attorney James L. Pugh, jr., has strong reasons for opposing the feeding of prisoners en masse in the dingy and darksome police court cages, and his reasons are good ones.

In the first place, he said last evening, I most certainly believe the prisoners locked up overnight in the police stations should be provided with breakfasts, but not in the foul cages in the rear of the court, which are only four feet wide by six feet deep. Into each of these cells there are frequently dumped in the early mornings from twenty to thirty culprits, embracing men of tender feelings and stomachs as well as the hardened vag, the foul smelling tramp or the soiled and odoriferous drunk. The condition of these cages after they have been occupied for only few moments by the human beings packed like sardines is simply terrible. The stone floors are covered with tobacco juice and other excretions, not to mention the foul odors from the closet in the wall, one of which is in each cell. I contend that it is inhuman to feed human beings in such manner and place. I would far rather eat my meals in an open air hog pen than in the tightly-closed, foul-smelling police court cages.

The plan I would suggest is to give the several station houses in the early morning. There is no van which goes to a station house earlier than 6 o'clock. Each precinct has an arrangement with some caterer for feeding the prisoners on Sunday. The same parties could serve them in the morning, and then each prisoner would get his breakfast in his cell alone and not surrounded by men in every degree of uncleanliness.

Another thing, the number of prisoners at single station usually range from five to ten. How much easier would it be to feed them in severalty at the stations than to wait until they reach court, where there are from twenty-five to one hundred prisoners huddled together. This would save confusion after the men have reached the cages and simplify the matters generally. In other words, the service at the court should be distributed to the nine precincts and then when the court is reached the men would be ready for trial and there would be no commission of breakfast dishes to be washed as it were.

ATLANTA. February 12.—The annual convention of the Hebrew benevolent association, B'nai B'rith, for the district composed of the States of Georgia, North and South Carolina, Virginia and Maryland and the District of Columbia, met this morning at 10 o'clock in Atlanta. It is attended by prominent Hebrews from all parts of the district and will be in session to-day and to-morrow. The morning session was devoted only to the preliminary work and the convention will assemble again this afternoon.

Hon. Simon Wolf, of Washington, D. C., the president of this district, is president. Among other leading Hebrews here are Hon. Julius Straus, first vice president of the Grand Lodge; Max Cohen and Henry Adler, of Washington; A. Gunst and H. Whitlock, of Richmond; John Jay Cohen, of Augusta; J. Herman and Sol Baker, of Baltimore; J. Loeb, of Charleston; S. Herman, of Savannah, and others.

Washington City, Sept. 6.—Official confirmation of news of the victorious entry of Gen. Alfaro with his army into the city of Quito, Ecuador, has been received here. It came to the navy department in a dispatch from Commander Watson, of the United States steamer Ranger, now at Guayaquil. The dispatch is very brief, merely announcing the fact of the arrival of Gen. Alfaro, and saying that great enthusiasm prevails.

The dispatch gives definite and final official confirmation to the reports of the success of the revolution. The conflict has lasted several months, and the reports of Alfaro's movements have been so contradictory as to occasion doubts as to the success of his movements. But Commander Watson's dispatch removes all doubt, and shows that the rebellion has culminated in a revolution.

PROCURATION TO THE SYNDICATE FOR BONDS

PROBABLY NOT MORE THAN $50,000,000

TO COME FROM EUROPE.

J. Pierpont Morgan and August Belmont, who
are the leading members of the syndicate which
will furnish the Treasury with gold for bonds, re-
turned from Washington yesterday. Mr. Morgan
would not discuss the terms of the BOND agreement
or make any comments on the situation. Mr.
Belmont had this to say: THE object of the trans-
action is not the mere purchase and sale of bonds
but is to assist the Treasury in carrying out the
object for which it is in existence—the acquiring
of gold and keeping it there by the best means at
its disposal. Naturally, then, one object of the
syndicate will be to prevent gold being withdrawn
from the Treasury for the purchase of the bonds.
Of course it follows that every one who is in
the syndicate must have the same object in
view.

Applications have already been received by the
syndicate for the bonds but it is not likely that
any but a few banks and some foreign banking
houses will be allowed in the syndicate. Deposits
of gold were made in some banks yesterday, pre-
sumably for the bonds, but it could not be learned
how soon gold would be turned into the Sub-Treas-
ury. By the language of the President's message

ance for ten days in the hope of authority from

The official memorandum of the contract for the
sale of the bonds made by the Administration
and the Morgan Belmont syndicate, was as follows:

The contract was made with August Belmont &
Co. of New-York, on behalf of Messrs N. M.
Rothschild & Sons, of London and themselves and

S. Morgan & Co. of London, and themselves, and
provides for the delivery to the United States of
500,000 ounces of standard gold coin of the United

but their names not mentioned in the contract
itself. This department does not know in what
proportions the various parties are to furnish the
gold coin and receive the bonds as this is a matter
for arrangement between themselves. By the
terms of the contract the parties are to bear all
the expense of bringing gold from abroad, and they
are so far as lies in their power, to exert all
their financial influence, and make all legitimate
efforts to secure the delivery of gold pending complete performance of the con-
tract. No bonds to be delivered except in pay-
ment for gold actually delivered. In view of the
possible failure of legislation in Congress, nego-
tiations have been pending for some time here and
abroad and the terms of this contract are the best
that could be procured with coin for bonds.

$17.50 an ounce. The gold is worth at the Assay

tional and the American Exchange. The gold hold-
ings of all the city banks are about $4,000,900.

gold will come from Europe.

STRATTONVILLE, VA. April 2.—Special—The death of Mr. John L. Brady occurred here this morning at about 8 o'clock. He had been thought to be much better and in fact his friends thought he might possibly weather it through and get over his spell. Feeling so much better, he with his wife's assistance, walked a few steps into the yard and back, which fatigued him very much. He then undertook to lie down, and in few minutes he was dead. principal, had no exercises, the scholars
being dismissed on account of the very
large number of visitors expected. The
class exhibits here of penmanship, class
work, drawings and sewing are especially
fine. The blackboard drawings in colors,
by Wesley Heinel are deserving OF men-
tion as being most artistic and well exc-
ecuted and shows signs of great promise in
future. In one of the girls rooms there
is fine drawing of thimble, emery
bag and needle and thread. Other pretty
drawings by the same lad are country
scenes, light houses, &c. In the school
work it would be hard to discriminate.
Nothing in the exhibit was prepared for
the occasion, but papers good, bad and
indifferent of each pupils term work are
shown. The drawings of Robert Baldwin,
Herbert Watson and Fred Macklin, were
very good. A map of the United States
by Jennie Y. Tatman, would need close
inspection to tell it was not cut out of II
geography, the coloring and lettering
being nearly perfect. Esther N. J. Kaig and
Lizzie W. Hamilton also show some nice
work. The sewing exhibit embraces "sam-
plers," aprons from gingham to lawn,
hemstitched handkerchiefs, embroidered
doylies, bureau and table scarfs, dolls,
and underwear, and is very creditable indeed.
All the rooms also make cabinet displays
of folded paper work.


But the chief point of interest OF
the afternoon was at No. 4 school, Miss
Francis, principal. Interesting exercises
were held at 3 o'clock in Miss MCCARTHY
room, where on the wall behind the plat-
form were draped the Stars and Stripes
made by the girl pupils. The flag is 9x12
feet in size and represents a great amount
of painstaking labor, indeed, the stripes
having been sewn and felled so neatly one
must look closely to see that it is not
woven, the stars cut and herring-boned to
the blue. It was regular jubilee day among
the girls of No. 4. Edgar Rawlins carved a
piece of wood to represent a cord pile and
the half and quarter sections. A leaf
carved in relief on a flat block, the work
of William Bicking, was much admired.
A miniature chair, about 4 inches high,
made by Howard Oberly, also came in to
its share of attention. The sewing, draw-
ing and class work exhibits of this schoo-
l are very fine.

I think a blush would have been more becoming, but they own their faces and that's their business."

Bayard—"How do you account for the detection of these men?"

Clayton—"Well, you see, Townsend has a brother named Tim who wanted state auditor. Burton had a friend named Edgar T. Hastings who wanted to be clerk of the House. Both Tim and Edgar were willing to sacrifice their private interests in the service of the state. You have probably noticed, Jim, that down here in Dover you occasionally run across men who are of that unselfish character. To resume the thread of my discourse, the Higgins lieutenants needed the eight votes of New Castle county and two of the Sussex votes to make up ten, the number requisite for a majority of the Republican caucus. First, they tried moral suasion on Townsend and Burton; it wouldn't work. Then they tried offices. That argument was one which was both agreeable and convincing. They knew what it meant, and they were no up on the ramifications of moral suasion. Townsend says, 'Make my brother Tim state auditor and I will vote for Higgins for United States senator. I know Tim; the caucus has been held at Harrington,' said Burton, 'but that doesn't matter; I have a friend down here in Dover who wants to be clerk of the House. His name is Hastings. He has the prerequisites from a plain hand with whiskers for the wind to blow through. If you will pull the wires for him I will vote for Higgins. I may also want to name one of the county officers of Sussex, but that...' After a consideration, McMullen walked into Higgins's office and said, 'Gentlemen, I want to be speaker of the House and I don't care who knows it. I know you have Fred Pyle slated for the place and that the Addicks-Massey end of the machine is ready to put up Charlie Moore; but I'm going to have it, or Senator Higgins cannot have my vote. I may also want to be clerk of New Castle county but that I am willing to leave to the future. How faithful to Senator Higgins will you be if we make you speaker?' asked the Higgins managers. 'Make me speaker and I will vote for Higgins for two weeks.' FROM THE SOUTH—A LIGHT MOVEMENT.


The cotton market was erratic yesterday. Opening 10 points up, it further advanced points, declined 15 points, rallied and closed steady at a net loss of 2 points. This market followed LIVERPOOL which after strong opening lost more than half of the improvement. The decline abroad was said by private cables to be due to the intention of Manchester mills to go on short time on account of the poor condition of trade. Silver declined. William Mohr, leading bear, who has just got back from Liverpool, heavily early. The small fry and speculators followed his lead. The sellers turned buyers, however, in the last hour, the weekly totals showing the movement of the crop were posted.
